The Messenger of God (peace be upon him) grew angry until anger was seen in his face, and said: "As for me, I fast and I break my fast, and I stand in prayer and I sleep, and I marry women; so whoever turns away from my way is not of me." He forbade those who wanted celibacy — among them ʿUthman ibn Mazʿun, may God be pleased with him — forbidding them that most severely and rebuking them for it.

He likewise forbade al-Hawlaʾ bint Tuwayt. She was a woman of the Banu Taym ibn Murrah upon whom Abu Bakr used to spend; she would stand the whole night in prayer and not sleep, and would fast the whole year. She came to visit ʿAʾishah, may God be pleased with her, and the Messenger of God (peace be upon him) entered and said: "Who is this?" She said: "So-and-so" — mentioning her prayer and her fasting, that is, ʿAʾishah was praising her. The Messenger of God (peace be upon him) said: "Enough. Take upon yourselves of deeds what you are able for; God does not tire until you tire." "Take upon yourselves of deeds what you are not able for" — its meaning is: strive to perform of righteous deeds only what you are able for, and do not burden yourselves with what you are not able for.

He said to ʿAbd Allah ibn ʿAmr ibn al-ʿAs, when he was a strong young man who used to fast every day and stand in prayer most of the night, forbidding him that: "Your eye has a right upon you, and your guest has a right upon you, and your wife has a right upon you; so give to everyone who has a right his right." He ordered him to fast three days of every month, and he said: "I can do more than that." So he ordered him to fast two days of the week, Monday and Thursday, and he said: "I can do more than that." So he ordered him to fast the fast of David, fasting a day and breaking the fast a day. When ʿAbd Allah grew old and his body weakened he said: "Would that I had taken the dispensation of the Messenger of God (peace be upon him)."

Likewise he (peace be upon him) made the matter clear to the Mothers of the Believers when they went into retreat: he saw that the tents had multiplied in the mosque, and it occurred to him that this might be for other than God, so he said: "Is it piety you think of them?" When he entered on the twentieth day of Ramadan wanting to enter his place of retreat, he saw the tents in the mosque and said: "What is this?" It was said: "The Mothers of the Believers are in retreat." He said: "Is it piety you think of them?"

For that reason a man must know that excessive exertion in discharging God's right, over against the suspending of the rights of human beings, is not part of uprightness upon the correct way, nor is it part of travelling the centre of the road. It is soundly established from him (peace be upon him) that he saw a man of the Ansar keeping to the mosque, and he asked who provided for him. It was said: "His brother." So he said that his brother was better than he — his brother who works and strives and gathers wealth from what is lawful for him and spends upon this brother of his is better than he. This requires that the moderate believer who earns and spends upon those whose maintenance is incumbent upon him is better than the one who cuts himself off for worship and so becomes a burden upon others and a dependent upon them.

From this we know that if a man wants to go to excess in worship and to pass beyond the limit, then at that point no one strains at this religion but that it overcomes him: the religion will overcome him, and a time must come in which he weakens before his body, or before his mind, or before his soul, or before his appetite, or before an illness that afflicts him; and he must also be struck with discouragement from the abundance of what befalls him. Hence it happened to some of those who entered by this door and went to excess in it that a man used to suppose his station very high, and then, when death came to him, he regretted it with the utmost regret, and there appeared to him from God what he had not reckoned with.

So whoever wants to go to excess in worship and pass beyond the limit in it must be afflicted with one of several things. Either he despises the straight way, and so wants to add to what the Messenger of God (peace be upon him) and his Companions were upon — and this is the utmost of far-going error. Hence Ibn Masʿud said: "Every act of worship that the Companions of Muhammad (peace be upon him) did not worship by, do not worship by it; for the first left no ground for the last to speak on." The maxim of the people of the Sunnah and the community is: "Had it been good, they would have preceded us to it" — which is the reverse of the maxim of the idolaters. The idolaters say: "Had it been good, they would not have preceded us to it"; and the people of the Sunnah say: "Had it been good, they would have preceded us to it." Every good is certainly in what the Messenger of God (peace be upon him) brought and acted upon and his Companions acted upon, may God's good pleasure be upon them, and it is not possible for the later ones to bring anything better than what they brought. Hence Malik, may God have mercy on him, said: "The last of this community will not be set right except by what set right its first."

Or he is afflicted with another matter, namely innovating, in that he legislates what God has not permitted. He supposes that the religion is deficient and that he himself is completing it out of his own resources; and this man is a partner of the first in plain error, because he has claimed that God Most High does not know what would complete and perfect His religion, and so he has come to complete it by his own independent reasoning out of his own resources. Al-Shatibi, may God have mercy on him, mentioned that the greatest of what is wrong in innovations is that their author supposes he is completing the religion, and that the religion was deficient before his own independent reasoning, and that he has brought something new by which he completes the religion that Muhammad (peace be upon him) brought — so he is claiming that the words of God Most High, "Today I have perfected your religion for you," are not correct. We ask God for safety and well-being.

Or he is afflicted with another thing, namely conceit: he goes to excess in worship and supposes himself to have reached a high station, and Satan may make it appear to him that the obligations have been lifted from him, and that it is open to him to fall into abominations and acts of disobedience, supposing thereby that he has reached a station in which he is not harmed by disobedience — as the Jews claimed who said, "The Fire will not touch us except for a number of days." This state is a treading of their road; and the Prophet (peace be upon him) made clear that there must be in this community those who tread their road. He said: "You will surely follow the ways of those before you, a span by a span, until if they entered the hole of a lizard you would follow them." They said: "Messenger of God, the Jews and the Christians?" He said: "Who else?" So the Jews who said, "The Fire will not touch us except for a number of days" — their traces have been followed by those of this community who are extreme in worship, who claim that they have reached a station in which God will not punish them. Indeed some of them reach the point of audacity towards God, so that one says: "If God threw me into the Fire it would be extinguished." We ask God for safety and well-being. This is the utmost deviation and distance from the straight road and from this highway.

Rather, he may be afflicted with another matter, namely that he claims to have reached a station in which the worshipper is united with the One worshipped — which is what they call the unity of being (waḥdat al-wujūd), or the station of indwelling, or the unity of unity, or union, or the unity of witnessing. All of these are technical terms that go back to this same idea in its origin, even if there are fine distinctions between them. They claim that a man, at that point, when he has known, certainty has come to him, and they interpret the words of God Most High, {And worship your Lord until certainty comes to you} (Sūrat al-Ḥijr 15:99), in this sense. This is the utmost error and misunderstanding, for certainty is death: "worship your Lord until certainty comes to you" means until death comes to you. Those who claim here that certainty comes to them — that is, a known station that they reach — have deviated most deviantly and strayed from the level road, and Satan has led them by their halters into plain unbelief. We ask God for safety and well-being.

The one who goes to excess in worship may also be afflicted with another thing, namely disparagement: Satan makes it seem to him that all his work is unaccepted with God, and that consequently his performing the work and his leaving it are the same; and from here he will abandon the work on this ground. Rather he may be afflicted with obsessive scruple about sincerity, so that he supposes every work to be insincere and keeps repeating the prayer and repeating the ablution — as you see the scrupulous, one of whom, when he washes his face, can hardly finish it. Those who go to excess in acts of worship are struck with kinds of affliction; those who pass beyond the limit set by the Law are struck with many kinds of affliction of this sort.

And on the opposite side, the deficient — those of neglect in worship — are the ones afflicted with inclining to the left from this path. They forget the wisdom for which they were created, and forget that they were created only for the worship of God, and so they are neglectful in His worship and fall short in it, and they entertain wishes about God and hang upon conjectures. For that reason Satan lures them into falling into acts of disobedience to God, and reminds them only of the verses of promise and the hadiths of promise, and they forget the verses of threat. Such people leave at first the recommended acts, then they leave the sunnah acts, then that brings them to leaving some of the obligatory acts, then that brings them to leaving the pillars, then that brings them to an evil end at death. We ask God for safety and well-being.

Every falling short and abandonment of worship is an occasion for a man to take a deficiency and a falling short in the station above that from which he has subtracted. If a man falls short in the regular prayers attached to the obligatory ones, then scratches must occur in the prayer. What people complain of — dryness of the eyes, so that when the Qur'an is recited they do not weep, though if it were recited to the mountains water would burst from them, if it were recited to the mountains they would weep, {had We sent down this Qur'an upon a mountain, you would have seen it humbled, splitting apart from the fear of God; and these similitudes We strike for people, that they may reflect} (Sūrat al-Ḥashr 59:21) — its cause is falling short in worship. And what people complain of, the absence of humility in the prayer, its cause is falling short in the voluntary prayers. You know that many people are still and composed in the obligatory prayer in a way they are not in the voluntary: when one of them wants to pray a voluntary prayer he pecks at it, and takes no care over it, not even in facing the qiblah, nor in turning aside, nor in failing to straighten the back in bowing, and so on; and when he wants to perform the obligatory prayer he tries to perfect it. But he cannot perfect the obligatory prayer while his voluntary prayer is like this, for the voluntary is the fence of the obligatory, and every scratch in it will reach the obligatory. Hence the scholars likened the voluntary prayer — and especially the regular prayers attached to the obligatory ones — to the bark of a stick: if the bark is stripped off, the stick dries up. The bark is the rind; if it is stripped off, the stick dries up.

Those who fall short in the worship of God, glorified and exalted, cannot be among His friends, because His friends are those who find intimacy with Him, glorified and exalted; they do not grieve when people grieve, for when calamities come they know that they are from God and that they were written before they came to be, and they are content with what God has decreed. And when ease and prosperity come, they are not deluded by that, knowing that it too was written and has an appointed term: {No calamity befalls in the earth or in yourselves but it is in a Book before We bring it into being — truly that is easy for God — so that you may not grieve over what has escaped you, nor exult over what He has given you} (Sūrat al-Ḥadīd 57:22-23).

Those who fall short in this worship cannot taste the savour of the particular service of the Compeller, glorified and exalted, nor feel the favour of being ascribed to Him, glorified and exalted. For that reason there must be found in them a great deal of harshness, coarseness of temper, ill dealing, and ill manners towards God, glorified and exalted, and towards His Messenger, and towards His Law. They do not respect the Qur'an, and they do not esteem the Sunnah, and they do not respect the symbols of God or magnify them: {That — and whoever magnifies the symbols of God, it is from the piety of hearts} (Sūrat al-Ḥajj 22:32). For that reason people do not love one another for God's sake: if they see one who worships God, glorified and exalted, and loves Him and esteems Him and calls to Him, they do not love him; they do not find in their souls any love for him, because the affective side in their dealing with God has been broken in them, and so they do not know love for God's sake. Love for God's sake arises only from uprightness upon the way and holding to His worship. If you know that you fall short of discharging God's right which He deserves of worship, then you love Gabriel and Michael, because they worship God with the worship He deserves; and you love every worshipper of God, because he discharges the right you wish to discharge and are unable to.

Likewise, those who fall short in worship are struck with other diseases, among the greatest of them audacity in disobedience. For the worshipper of God, glorified and exalted, is restrained by his worship from disobedience. God Most High said: Truly the prayer restrains from indecency and wrong, and the remembrance of God is greater, and God knows what you do. The one who does not find this wall between himself and disobedience is under one coverlet with disobedience: he finds himself with it at every hour. Whereas the one who is in worship has a mighty wall between himself and disobedience, and from here his limbs do not yield to disobedience. Even if Satan causes him to slip into it, it cannot continue, as He said, exalted is He: {Truly those who are God-fearing, when a visitation from Satan touches them, remember, and at once they see clearly} (Sūrat al-Aʿrāf 7:201).

Likewise, falling short in worship requires of a man that his aspiration not be high and that he be content with the lowest of stations. Whoever has high aspiration wants to increase every day — indeed every hour — in nearness to God, and to be among those who compete for the highest degrees of the Garden, and to be among those whose sides shun their beds at the time of sleep, remembering the race, and that God, glorified and exalted, has now opened the contest for His servants. So whoever is not forsaken by God is among those racing to Him with acts of obedience at this hour, in which the doors of worship have been opened, and in which the Sovereign, the Requiter, has given leave for intimate speech to those who would speak intimately with Him, and has shut no door between Himself and them, and has let down no veil before them, and has lowered no valleys and raised no mountain passes. So they race one another in drawing near to Him: {Those whom they call upon themselves seek the means of approach to their Lord, which of them shall be nearest, and they hope for His mercy and fear His punishment — truly the punishment of your Lord is a thing to be guarded against} (Sūrat al-Isrāʾ 17:57); {Truly they used to hasten to good works and call upon Us in longing and in fear, and they were humble before Us} (Sūrat al-Anbiyāʾ 21:90).

The one who falls short in worship in his ordinary times, when the time of hardship comes, is not among those whose supplications are answered at that time, because he did not make himself known to God in ease: "Make yourself known to God in ease, and He will know you in hardship." Those who fall short in worship do not become leaders or masters of the believers; and God, glorified and exalted, has directed us to make this supplication: {And those who say: our Lord, grant us from our wives and our offspring the coolness of eyes, and make us a leader for the God-fearing} (Sūrat al-Furqān 25:74).

There must be, then, an adherence to the middle way, in which there is neither excess nor neglect on the side of worship. A man should know that the best worship is the worship of Muhammad (peace be upon him), and that that worship is varied by the variety of circumstance and is ordered upon times and seasons. What the Messenger of God (peace be upon him) used to say in the morning, try to say it in the morning; and what he used to say in the evening, try to say it in the evening; and what he used to do at bedtime when he went to his bed, try to do it; and what he used to do in standing at night, try to do it; and what he used to do of the regular prayers, and what he used to do at home and on journey of acts of worship, try to perform it. In that way you will have held to the centre of the road, finding nothing that wearies your body, nor anything that wearies your mind, nor anything that wearies your spirit; and neither will you be one who falls short — rather you will be among those who increase in nearness, who travel at a steady pace that leads to the goal without haste, with all deliberation and gentleness.

This is what God and His Messenger (peace be upon him) love, as the Messenger of God (peace be upon him) said to the Ashajj of ʿAbd al-Qays: "In you are two qualities that God and His Messenger love: forbearance and deliberateness." So if a man is deliberate in his worship, performing it with truthfulness and sincerity and presence of mind, and burdening himself with what he is capable of and able for, and is not of those who want to burn up the distances and cut the road in the quickest times — who neither leave a mount alive nor cover any distance — then by that he will arrive, God Most High willing, at the station approved with God, and will continue in increase and ascent throughout his life. And if he becomes unable to do something, it is written for him complete, as he used to do it in his health, as the Messenger of God (peace be upon him) made clear: God Most High says to His angels, when the servant falls ill or travels: "Look at what My servant used to do in his health and at home, and write it for him." God, glorified and exalted, does not tire until you tire; and He has no need of us and of our worship, and we cannot draw near to Him by what He has not laid down for us. The one who can be harmed by you and benefited by you — you can draw near to him with a benefit he did not command you with, and you can remove from him a harm he did not command you to remove. But the One who can be neither benefited nor harmed by you — you cannot draw near to Him except by what He has laid down for you and made clear, and you cannot pass beyond that in any circumstance whatever.

Likewise, on the side of dealings, we must know that the most divisive thing for hearts in dealings is what relates to money. In the gathering of money there must be a middle course: neither excess nor neglect. Those who are excessive in gathering it and spend their hours in gathering it will lose precious hours and rare opportunities for acts of worship. The one who remains the whole of his day occupied with striking bargains in the markets will miss the hours when supplications are answered; he will miss the hour of the descent; he will sleep through the hours in which the race takes place among the worshippers racing towards God, {and in that let the competitors compete} (Sūrat al-Muṭaffifīn 83:26); he will miss the first row on many occasions; he will miss the waiting at the frontier; "the ones who go on ahead have outstripped"; he will miss much good.

The one who goes to excess in gathering money and gathering the refuse of this world and occupying himself with it is struck with a number of afflictions. First, that this world becomes great in his soul, so that it becomes the greatest of his aims and the utmost of his knowledge, and his heart becomes occupied with it and fills with it, even if his hand is empty of it. For those occupied with this world are not necessarily rich: many of the rich have this world in their hands and not in their hearts, and many of the poor do not have this world in their hands but have it in their hearts. Therefore what the Law warns against is the attachment of the heart to it, and that a man make it the greatest of his concerns and the extent of his knowledge, and that he be a worshipper of it, his service and his striving being for its sake. This is the annihilating danger, and it is a great harm to its possessor, because it leads him to the point of transgression and tyranny. God Most High said: {Truly man is tyrannous when he sees himself grown rich} (Sūrat al-ʿAlaq 96:6-7); and He said, exalted is He: {And had God expanded provision for His servants they would have transgressed in the earth, but He sends down in a measure what He wills} (Sūrat al-Shūrā 42:27). So transgression, tyranny and passing beyond the limit come about only by going to excess in gathering this world.

On the opposite side, we must also know that falling short in gathering it is a deficiency in a man. The one who turns away from it altogether and does not want to manage anything of the affairs of this world, nor to earn anything, is outside the correct way and has not travelled the road of the Messenger of God (peace be upon him). For the Messenger (peace be upon him) took the means and put them to work and did not leave them. Had the renunciation of this world which the Law praises required the abandoning of means and cutting oneself off for worship and monasticism, the Messenger of God (peace be upon him) and his Companions would have done it. Since they did not do it — and we find among them the merchants, and we find among them the rich, and we find among them those who spend in the way of God; and we find the endowments of the Messenger of God (peace be upon him) from which thousands of widows and orphans were maintained; and we find that he stored up a year's provision for his household; and we find that he (peace be upon him) was granted by God the land of the Banu al-Nadir as spoil and stored up some of it for his dependants; and we find that he (peace be upon him) used to plant palms with his own hand — may my father and mother be his ransom — and used to draw water, may my father and mother be his ransom (peace be upon him); and he helped in the planting of Salman's palms, for which his masters had made a contract of manumission with him; and we saw him going to the markets and buying and walking in them, which is what the idolaters found objectionable in him and which God endorsed for him in His Book.

And we saw his Companions — and they are the best of the people of the earth by the testimony of the Messenger of God (peace be upon him) for them — and among them were the merchants, such as Abu Bakr, may God be pleased with him, who spent upon his dependants from the yield of his trade. His capital was four hundred dirhams, and he used to trade with it in cloth — that is, garments — and in oil; and whatever he gained he spent upon those he maintained. And Abu Bakr's dependants were many poor families. We find among them likewise ʿAbd al-Rahman ibn ʿAwf, who was God's merchant in this earth: God blessed him in his transactions, so he spent upon many orphans and needy people, and he bequeathed a third of his wealth to the survivors of the people of Badr, so that it was riches for them all. We find among them al-Zubayr ibn al-ʿAwwam, whose investments were in wide lands and great farms, and who left much wealth, the price of which, divided among his wives, was riches for them. Among them is Abu Talhah al-Ansari, who had a great deal of farmland and owned Bayruhaʾ, which was the finest farm in Medina, and he used to pray two units of prayer beneath every palm tree. We find among them Saʿd ibn ʿUbadah ibn Dulaym, who was among the great merchants and the rich, who when they returned from the forenoon prayer went to their farms, and when the day had risen high went to their trades; and when the time of the sun's decline came they occupied themselves with prayer and with preparing for the obligatory prayer; and when they returned from it they discharged the right of their families. They apportioned their hours in this apportionment and nothing of the good escaped them.

When we know that, we know that the moderate way requires the absence of excess and the absence of neglect. So the one who supposes that the renunciation of this world which the Law praises requires of him that he not occupy himself with gathering this world is a liar, at variance with the correct way; he has only travelled the road of the Jews and the Christians who invented a monasticism out of themselves. And the one who supposes that God does not approve for His servants the gathering of this world from what is lawful in it is a liar, because God Most High created for us all that is in the earth and said: {So walk in its tracts and eat of His provision} (Sūrat al-Mulk 67:15). He made us successors in the earth, and said: {Truly I am placing in the earth a successor} (Sūrat al-Baqarah 2:30). And He commanded us to set it right and not to corrupt it after its setting right. All of this requires of us that we work and that we do what is right in this earth. But with all that, we must know that setting it right, and gathering it, does not require that it be in the hearts; rather it should be in the hands, according to the way set out above.

Those who are excessive on the side of gathering money are struck with afflictions, among the greatest of them servitude to the created being. For man is constituted upon need — man's very self is poverty: {O people, you are the poor in need of God, and God is the Self-Sufficient, the Praiseworthy} (Sūrat Fāṭir 35:15). From here, if a man shrinks from engaging in this world altogether and does no work that yields him his maintenance, he is a slave to another; for the one who spends upon him has every pressure over him, since he fears him and loves him and may obey him on many occasions. For that reason, realising servitude to God requires independence from created beings — that a man find that no one has any pressure over him, so that neither fear nor greed turns him back from speaking the truth and from servitude to God, glorified and exalted. In that way a man can free himself from what is other than God; and so long as a man does not do that, he is a follower of another and a dependant of another, in need of one who manages his affairs at all his hours.

Likewise, among what the one excessive in worldly affairs is afflicted with is that his soul and his heart often become attached to it, so that he is afflicted with love of it without noticing; and even if he puts on an outward show and displays to people that he does not love it, his heart inclines to it. From here we witness today the people of the church making a show of cutting themselves off from this world while they are the most deeply plunged in it: indeed hardly a short period passes but their scandals are announced in the media. In the first age too they used to gather wealth and hoard it, before the sending of the Messenger of God (peace be upon him); and the Prophet (peace be upon him) set out stories of that.

Those who cut themselves off, as it appears to people, are often approached by Satan from the direction of doubts and from the direction of appetites; and they are often struck with a weakness in the mind that lets Satan find them weak. So he whispers whisperings to them, and visions are imagined for one of them in his waking state, so that he sees that he saw such-and-such while awake and not asleep — and they are dreams and visions, weaker than the visions of sleep. The waking visions that come to a man when he has gone hungry, or fallen ill, or exhausted himself with ascetic exercises: he sees while awake the like of what he sees in sleep — like one struck with malarial fever in his waking state, who raves as though he were dreaming while he is awake and not asleep. So too the one who has exhausted himself in acts of worship and has not travelled the level road that the Prophet (peace be upon him) brought is struck with raving, and sees dreams while awake, and it is imagined to him that they are true and that so-and-so came to him, and that he saw the Prophet (peace be upon him), or Gabriel, or the Preserved Tablet, or the like — and all of these are waking dreams: when he grew very weak, Satan made that appear to him. Some of them may be genuine visions, but they are of a weaker degree than the vision of sleep — the vision of sleep is stronger than they — because at that point he is stronger in his body and his mind than he is when weakened in the waking state.

Likewise, the one who goes to excess in cutting himself off from this world is often struck with neglect of the rights of others: he is neglectful of the rights of his body in health care and cleanliness, neglectful in the care of his family, neglectful in paying his debts and discharging what is due from him. All these matters he neglects, while Satan deludes him that what he is upon is correct; and the more his years increase upon him, the further he goes from the highway and the straight path.

Likewise, another of these aspects relates to money, namely its spending. This religion is a middle religion between excess and neglect. God Most High said: {And those who, when they spend, are neither extravagant nor niggardly, but there is a just mean between that} (Sūrat al-Furqān 25:67). Those who are extravagant are the excessive, who go too far in spending money and put it in other than its lawful place, as though it were their property to dispose of where they will and how they will — when in fact it is a trust from God, glorified and exalted, in which He has made them successors so as to see how they act. Hence God taught His Messenger (peace be upon him) the finest manners upon this upright way, and said: {And do not make your hand shackled to your neck, nor stretch it out to the utmost} (Sūrat al-Isrāʾ 17:29). So a man must be in the middle in spending, and must not be extravagant and must not be deficient either; the middle limit is the correct way, and that is moderation in this chapter.

Those who are excessive on the side of spending are extravagant and go to excess in spending, whether that be in worldly matters or in matters of the hereafter, and so they pass beyond the limit approved in the Law. In matters of the hereafter they spend more than the Lawgiver has set, wanting thereby to go to excess, and so they come back to the limit we mentioned in the case of excess in worship. For that reason the Messenger of God (peace be upon him), when he heard that Thabit ibn Qays ibn Shammas, may God be pleased with him, had spent the whole harvest of his palms in a single day, was severely angry with him. And when he heard that a man of the Ansar who had a debt upon him had made six slaves conditionally free upon his death, and had died, the Messenger of God (peace be upon him) gathered them and rejected this disposition and drew lots among them, and freed two and left four in slavery — he allowed him the third only. Often he rejected certain dispositions in this aspect when there was exaggeration and excess in them.

He said to Kaʿb ibn Malik, when he proposed it to him at his repentance, God having turned to him in forgiveness — the Messenger of God (peace be upon him) said to him, "Kaʿb ibn Malik, receive good tidings of the best day that has passed over you since your mother bore you." He said: "I said, Messenger of God, is it from God or from you?" He said: "Rather from God." He said: "I said, Messenger of God, part of the completeness of my repentance is that I give away all my wealth in the way of God." He said: "Keep back some of your wealth for yourself; it is better for you."

Likewise, when he came to visit Saʿd ibn Abi Waqqas during the Farewell Pilgrimage while he was ill, he said: "I said to him, Messenger of God, I am a man of wealth, and none inherits from me but a daughter of mine. Shall I give away all my wealth in charity in the way of God?" He said: "No." "I said: shall I give away two thirds of it in charity?" He said: "No." "I said: shall I give away a third of it in charity?" He said: "A third — and a third is much" — and in another transmission, "a third is great." "Truly, that you leave your heirs rich is better than that you leave them destitute, begging from people." "I said: Messenger of God, shall I be left behind after my companions?" He said: "Truly you will not spend any expenditure seeking thereby the face of God but that you are rewarded for it, even what you put into your wife's mouth. And it may be that God will benefit some peoples by you and harm others by you." Saʿd was the last of the Ten to die, and he was inherited from by twelve sons of his own loins among his children.

So the Messenger of God (peace be upon him) did not accept excess in spending from those men. On the opposite side, he may accept it from certain people, knowing the strength of their faith and their uprightness upon the way — as with Abu Bakr, who gave away all his wealth in the way of God, and the Messenger of God (peace be upon him) accepted that from him, because of the faith and contentment God had put in his heart, and because he was also an earner, acquainted with the affairs of trade, and because he would certainly discharge the rights of his dependants and could not possibly wrong them of a right due to them. For that reason the Messenger of God (peace be upon him) accepted that from him; whereas from others besides him the Messenger of God (peace be upon him) would reject it and would not accept this kind of excess from them.

Likewise, the one who goes to excess in spending in worldly matters must be among the squanderers, and they are the brothers of the devils; and this kinship is among the worst of kinships — for it is among the worst of kinships that a man be a brother to the devils. We ask God for safety and well-being. It is a bad relation. God, glorified and exalted, has made clear the harm of squandering and its great effect, and has made clear that He, glorified and exalted, does not love the extravagant. Hence the learned Muhammad Mawlud ibn Ahmad Fal, may God have mercy on him, said:

*Extravagance, extravagance! Truly extravagance — God Most High has forbidden it, and that is enough.*

*And "He does not love the extravagant" is sufficient to hold your hand back from extravagance.*

So it is enough, to hold your hand back from extravagance, that God does not love the extravagant: *and "He does not love the extravagant" is sufficient to hold your hand back from extravagance.*

Extravagance in worldly matters likewise requires of a man that this world become the greatest of his concerns and the extent of his knowledge, and that he love it with a fierce love, so that he follows its fashions and busies himself with it utterly; and thus, the more its firewood increases, the more its flame increases, and a man grows more infatuated with it and more attached in heart to it, until he prefers it to the hereafter. We ask God for safety and well-being. God Most High said: Whoever desires the harvest of the hereafter, We increase for him his harvest; and whoever desires the harvest of this world, We give him of it, and he has no share in the hereafter. And He said, exalted is He: And among people is one who says, our Lord, give us in this world — and he has no portion in the hereafter. And He said, exalted is He: Whoever desires the fleeting life, We hasten for him in it what We will for whom We intend; then We appoint for him Hell, which he shall enter, blamed and rejected. And whoever desires the hereafter and strives for it with its striving, being a believer — those, their striving is thanked.

Likewise, on the opposite side, falling short in the field of spending requires of a man miserliness, and that he be a miser who does not discharge the rights due from him. The one who withholds his gift, and eats alone, and beats his slave, is the worst of people, as the Messenger of God (peace be upon him) said: "The worst of people is he who withholds his gift, and eats alone, and beats his slave." This is the worst of people with God, mighty and majestic. "Whoever withholds his gift" means whoever withholds small kindnesses: he did not give his good to others and so did not benefit them from what God gave him. God, glorified and exalted, has commanded us to spend from what He has given us, and said: Believe in God and His Messenger, and spend of that in which He has made you successors. This includes spending upon oneself, upon one's family and upon one's neighbours, and spending in worldly matters and spending also in matters of religion; and abandoning it is part of falling short and of niggardliness, and both are blameworthy in the Law. The niggardly fall short of discharging the rights, and they are characterised by the trait of miserliness, which is the worst of traits. Whoever is characterised by it, whoever is afflicted with covetousness, must be afflicted — we ask God for safety and well-being — with a deficiency in faith and a constant regression in it. Hence God Most High said: And whoever is guarded against the covetousness of his own soul, those are the successful. So the covetous man never succeeds; the covetous, the miserly man never succeeds. For that reason there must be a middle course in this way between excess in spending and niggardliness and falling short.

Likewise on the side of character. Among the important matters is that a man should know that the straight way is this middle religion, which requires of a man that he make his character towards people good, in that he not be a mere follower, a copyist all of whose affairs are settled by others, and that he not be an arrogant, coarse man who obeys in nothing small or great. The middle limit requires of a man that he be positive and not negative, as the poet said:

*By your life, Abu Malik is no weakling, nor one of feeble strength,*

*nor a wrangler with a streak of folly in him, who baffles his brother when he forbids him.*

*If you lead him, you lead one readily obedient; and whatever you entrust to him, he suffices for it.*

And as another said:

*When the people make for his house, he sets himself to the best they thought of him, and he does it.*

*He pleases you when wronged, and satisfies you when he wrongs; whatever you load upon him, he carries.*

*A youth cut to the cut of a sword, neither shrunken nor flabby in his breast and his shoulders.*

This requires of a man completeness of personality, and that he not be a mere follower, imitating in the whole matter, such that he says: I heard people saying something, so I said it. And that he not be a harsh man whom people avoid for fear of his malice, for it has come from the Prophet (peace be upon him) that he said: "The worst of people is he whom people abandon in avoidance of his malice" — whom people abandon, or whom people beware of, in avoidance of his malice; he is the worst of people.

For that reason a man must be intent upon uprightness in character: that he not be among those who yield to everything and so accept innovations and accept wrong and keep silent at the sight of abominations, supposing that this is part of good character and modesty. This is a mistake; rather it is part of excess in modesty, until a man passes the limit. You, even if you are small, even if you are weak, are charged by God and are a soldier among God's soldiers; and from here you must guard the frontier post you hold, and Islam must not be entered from your side. So you must be watchful, and must be one who enjoins right and forbids wrong, whether you are great or small, rich or poor, learned or ignorant. You must uphold the right that is due from you to God, and must guard the religion in what is next to you, and must not let anything enter by this frontier post at which you stand — for you are a sentry on duty. And let not Satan deceive you with the claim of modesty: for the modesty that prevents the changing of a wrong, or the enjoining of right, or asking about a matter of religion, is the blameworthy modesty, odious in the Law, as the learned Muhammad Mawlud, may God have mercy on him, said:

*As for blameworthy modesty, it is that which prevents the changing of a wrong, or the asking about*

*a matter of the religion and the like; and it is what has been counted among the things that destroy.*

For that reason Umm Sulaym, may God be pleased with her, when she asked the Messenger of God (peace be upon him) about a woman who has a nocturnal emission and sees what a man sees, whether a full washing is incumbent upon her, said: "Truly God is not ashamed of the truth," and opened her speech with that. So a man must know that being ashamed of the truth is blameworthy and is not part of good and praiseworthy character; and he must know that currying favour with people and going along with them in what they are engaged in, and attending their gatherings even if there is in them what does not please God, and turning a blind eye to that, is not part of praiseworthy character. Rather praiseworthy character requires of a man that he bear patiently the harm of people in what concerns his own person; but he must be angry with God's anger when God's sanctities are violated. ʿAʾishah, may God be pleased with her, said: "The Messenger of God (peace be upon him) never avenged himself, and never was angry for his own sake; he was only angry with God's anger when God's sanctities were violated." This is what the believer is angry about: he is angry when God's sanctities are violated. As for his own rights, he overlooks them and is indulgent in them; but in the rights of God that is not accepted.

From this, excess in making one's character good and soft, to the point where a man can neither enjoin a right, nor forbid a wrong, nor speak the truth, nor take a correct stand — and where it produces embarrassment at speaking the truth and embarrassment at censuring a wrong — all this is part of blameworthy excess in which there is no good. And on the opposite side there is likewise neglect in character, in that a man is harsh, rough and coarse in the whole matter, even in God's own cause: if he enjoins a right he comes with coarseness and roughness, and if he forbids a wrong he comes with coarseness and roughness, as though he were a king over the necks of God's servants. This kind too is not approved with God; rather it is part of neglect in character. So a man must be mannered with the character God chose for His Messenger (peace be upon him): {It was by a mercy from God that you were gentle to them; had you been coarse and hard of heart they would have scattered from about you. So pardon them, and ask forgiveness for them, and consult them in the matter; and when you have resolved, then put your trust in God} (Sūrat Āl ʿImrān 3:159).

Neglect in character requires of a man that his manners be bad towards his parents, though they are the most trusted of people for him; and that his manners be bad towards his Muslim neighbours, though they have two rights, the right of neighbourhood and the right of Islam; and that his manners be bad towards the elders of the Muslims, whose honouring the Prophet (peace be upon him) made obligatory when he said: "My community will not cease to be in good so long as its elder shows mercy to its young and its young honours its elder." It requires bad manners likewise towards the angels who bear witness to his rebuking of the young and his trespassing upon rights; and it requires bad manners towards the Sovereign, the Requiter, glorified and exalted. So a man must remember God's power over him. Here is Abu Masʿud al-Badri, may God be pleased with him, who said: "I was flogging a slave of mine in the road, when there was a voice behind me saying: 'Know, Abu Masʿud.' I looked, and there was the Messenger of God (peace be upon him) saying: 'Know, Abu Masʿud, that God has more power over you than you have over this slave.' I said: 'Messenger of God, he is free for the sake of God.' He said: 'Truly, had you not done so, the Fire would have scorched you.'"

For that reason, neglect in character requires of a man that he be like the beasts in which there is no good, which have lost reason and so go headlong upon their faces caring for nothing. We ask God for safety and well-being. So a man must make his character good and discipline his soul and purify it, and that must be by the correct way and in accordance with the prophetic character.

Many people today, on the side of character, combine excess and neglect. On the side of excess, they are unable to censure a wrong or to change it, and claim that this is out of modesty; and on the side of neglect, they will not sit with certain elders — their in-laws, for instance — and will not eat with them, supposing that this is part of modesty and good character. And this is excess and the first is neglect; both things are odious in the Law. For had this been part of honouring elders, the Messenger of God (peace be upon him) and his Companions would have done it. The Messenger of God (peace be upon him) used to eat with Abu Bakr and ʿUmar and ʿAli and ʿUthman, and all of them were his in-laws; and he used to sit with them in their houses. He came to ʿAli and Fatimah while they were in their bed and said, "Stay where you are," when they wanted to rise to him, and he sat between them and put his back against Fatimah's belly and his feet against ʿAli's belly. ʿAli said: "I felt the coolness of his feet against my back." This is part of the manners of the Messenger of God (peace be upon him) and of his character; and no believer can turn away from the character of the Messenger of God (peace be upon him), or suppose that any character is better than his, ever, under any circumstance — because God Most High says: {And truly you are upon a mighty character} (Sūrat al-Qalam 68:4). So we cannot bring a character out of ourselves and have it be greater than the character of the Prophet (peace be upon him), or better; this is impossible.

For that reason, the one who does this kind of thing has combined the two base things, has combined excess and neglect; and this is widespread and common. I have learnt that in some environments here among us, regrettably, a man will not pray with his father-in-law in one mosque, and is unable to stand next to him in the row. This is part of excess in character and of exaggeration in it, and it is not sanctioned and has no ground from the point of view of the Law at all, in any way whatever. Nor does he visit him when he is ill, and he cuts him off completely — while God Most High says: {And among His signs is that He created for you, from yourselves, spouses that you may find rest in them, and He set between you love and mercy} (Sūrat al-Rūm 30:21). Where is the love and the mercy if a man cuts off his wife's family, and does not drink with them and does not eat, and does not visit their sick, and does not greet them, and cuts them off entirely? So this is not part of the character praised in the Law; rather it is part of odious excess in character.

We must know that this religion which God has approved for us enters into all the concerns of our life, and that the straight way in it prevents extremism. Extremism takes in both things: it takes in excess and neglect, for both of them are an extreme. Extremism (taṭarruf) is derived from the extreme (ṭaraf): *and both extremes of the due measure of affairs are blameworthy*. Excess and neglect are both of them extremism, odious in the Law. Today it has become common on the tongues of the media to apply "extremism" to the side of excess alone; and that is because those who apply it — the people of the media — are all of them among the neglectful, and so they are all of them extremists. They are all of them among the extremists, but they want to shift extremism to the other side only. The reality is that both extremes of the way are extremism.

Whoever knows this way, approved with God, glorified and exalted, and knows that it is the creed of the Messenger of God (peace be upon him), cannot turn himself away from it, for God Most High says: {And who turns away from the creed of Abraham but one who has made a fool of himself?} (Sūrat al-Baqarah 2:130). For that reason we must bring this way down into all our deeds, and must set before it the smallest of our affairs and our life and our actual situation.

Among the matters that ought to be set before this middle, straight way is what relates to dealing with women and mixing with them. In this aspect the straight way is that woman is the sister of man, and that between them is that cooperation in righteousness and God-fearing which has been laid down for them; and that each of them is charged, God having forbidden him or her things and made other things obligatory, and having set limits that cannot be transgressed; and that each of them is responsible for guarding this religion and aiding it; and that excess by passing beyond this way is odious, and that neglect by falling short of it is odious in the Law. People in this chapter, in the matter of mixing with women, combine both things, excess and neglect.

In the field of excess we find some people despising women and not respecting them as human beings and not esteeming them with this esteem, and not consulting women or seeking their legal opinions in matters of religion even if they are more learned and more sensible than he is — although God commanded them to teach people, and said: {And remember what is recited in your houses of the signs of God and the wisdom} (Sūrat al-Aḥzāb 33:34). And if a woman gives him a legal opinion he does not trust it. This is only excess in which there is no good, and neglect of the right of the woman herself. Like this, on the opposite side, is excess by passing beyond the limit in what relates to dealing with them, such as forbidden mingling and forbidden seclusion, and speech that raises suspicion, and softness of speech — and all of that is among what God has forbidden, and is among the limits outside the level, straight way.

We find also that some people in this field, in dealing with women, are excessive and exaggerate, so that one does not think it incumbent upon him to return the greeting to a woman if she greets him, and thinks that women likewise do not greet men and do not respond to a sneezer. So he speaks with the woman about worldly affairs, but if he sneezes she does not respond to him, and if he greets she does not return it to him and he does not return it to her. So the two of them have abandoned the obligatory thing commanded in the Law, which is among the rights of the Law, the rights of Islamic brotherhood; while he plunges into conversation and its byways — indeed the conversation the two of them plunge into may be something it is not lawful to plunge into at all, such as softness of speech and talk that raises suspicion. They talk in what raises suspicion, and neither of them returns the greeting to the other, nor responds when the other sneezes. There is no doubt that this combines excess and neglect.

We find that some people will not enter upon women in a house when they want to teach them, but put a partition between themselves and them, for instance, or order them to leave the mosque, or prevent them from going to the lessons, or prevent them from going to the lectures — and all of this is contrary to the prophetic way, for the Messenger of God (peace be upon him) said: "Do not prevent the maidservants of God from the mosques of God." He used to teach the women, and they used to sit with him. They said to him: "Messenger of God, I am the delegate of the women; they say that our brothers among the men have overcome us in your company, so appoint for us a day from yourself." So he appointed Thursday for them. The Messenger of God (peace be upon him) did not put a barrier between himself and the women; rather they used to pray with him in the mosque, and he used to say: "The best of the rows of the men is the first of them and the worst of them the last; and the best of the rows of the women is the last of them and the worst of them the first." He used to order the men not to leave until the women had left, and used to order the women not to raise their eyes until the men had sat up from prostration, lest anything of the men's nakedness be uncovered to them. They used to attend the dawn prayer with him, wrapped in their cloaks, not to be recognised in the darkness; and they used to attend with him the prayer of the Eid, the prayer for rain and the Friday prayers. In the hadith of Umm ʿAtiyyah: "We used to be commanded to bring out the young women, and the menstruating women, and those in seclusion, to witness the good and to swell the number of the Muslims."

The Messenger of God (peace be upon him) used to greet them and return the greeting to them and visit them when they fell ill, and his Companions used to do so. In Ṣaḥīḥ al-Bukhārī, Abu Bakr said to ʿUmar after the death of the Prophet (peace be upon him): "Come, let us visit Umm Ayman as the Messenger of God (peace be upon him) used to visit her." When the two of them entered upon her she wept, and they said to her: "Do you not know that what is with God is better for the Messenger of God (peace be upon him) than this world?" She said: "Indeed, I do not weep because I do not know that what is with God is better for the Messenger of God (peace be upon him) than this world; but I weep at the cutting off of revelation from heaven." So she stirred the two of them to weeping, and they wept, and then rose.

ʿUmar, may God be pleased with him, used to visit the old women of the Ansar and serve them; he used to milk the ewe for an old woman of the Ansar — he would milk her ewe for her. One night he went out patrolling and heard an old woman of the Ansar beating wool and saying:

*Upon Muhammad be the blessing of the righteous; may the good and the choice ones bless you.*

*You were one who stood long in prayer, weeping in the last hours of the night.*

*Would that I knew — and deaths come in turns — whether the abode will gather me and my beloved together.*

So ʿUmar sat down at her door weeping until the dawn broke. And the Messenger of God (peace be upon him) went out one night into one of the lanes of Medina and passed by the door of an old woman of the Ansar, and there she was reciting the Qur'an. The Messenger of God (peace be upon him) stood listening to her recitation, and she recited the words of God Most High: Has there come to you the account of the Overwhelming? And the Messenger of God (peace be upon him) said: "Yes, it has come to me; yes, it has come to me" — and he sat down weeping.

For that reason we must know that the straight way in mixing with women requires this: no excess in it and no neglect. We cannot follow out the particulars of this subject, but a hint is enough for the man of understanding. It is now known that the straight way is a middle way in all matters, their small ones and their great; and that excess in every matter is odious in the Law, and that neglect is blameworthy; and that every virtue lies between two vices. That has been recognised by the examples we have mentioned. We ask God, glorified and exalted, to make what we say and hear an argument for us and not against us, and to grant us success in what He loves and approves, and to make our whole work sincerely for His noble face. And may God bless and grant peace to our Prophet Muhammad and to his family and all his Companions.

flags.note: EDITORIAL REVIEW (house rule 12). Two passages carry reputational exposure in English. The first rejects the interfaith movement outright as a 'distorted religion' aimed at merging Islam, Judaism and Christianity, names the United States as its origin, and links it to colonial attempts on the religion. The second charges the Christian clergy as a body with hypocrisy about worldly goods and alludes to their scandals in the media. Both are translated at full strength, neither softened nor strengthened, and neither is omitted. The record also contains a sharp aside that everyone in the media is an extremist of the lax kind, and a criticism of a named local custom in Mauritania (a man refusing to pray beside his father-in-law). Whether and how to publish is for Ummah Collective and the Sheikh's office.

The lecture has a clear five-part shape: the principle of the middle way, then its application to belief, to worship, to dealings with money (gathering and then spending), to character, and finally to relations between men and women. The source marks none of these; each is introduced only by a transitional phrase inside the running block. The English keeps those phrases and adds no headings, since the Sheikh does not speak them. An editor building a display for this record will probably want headings, and these six transitions are where they belong.

translator_notes: Qur'anic renderings in this file are interpretive translations of meaning, offered to carry the Sheikh's argument in English. They are not a substitute for the Arabic text of the Qur'an.

A single public lecture on al-wasaṭiyyah, the middle way. The Sheikh sets out the principle from Sūrat al-Māʾidah 5:3 — that the religion is complete, so that every human addition is excess (ifrāṭ) and every subtraction is neglect (tafrīṭ) — and then applies it in turn to belief, to worship, to the gathering and the spending of money, to character, and to relations between men and women, showing at each point the disease at either extreme. The lecture is complete: it opens with the full formulas and closes with the customary supplication and blessing.

The source abbreviates the blessing upon the Prophet throughout as (ص). The English renders it in full as '(peace be upon him)' at every occurrence, which is the house convention in this corpus; the abbreviation is preserved unchanged in body_ar.

The term الإنترفيت is the English word 'interfaith' in Arabic letters, which the Sheikh glosses himself as الدين العالمي, 'the world religion'. The English gives the word he used, in quotation marks, with his own gloss following, rather than replacing it with a technical term he did not use.
